content: The transportation of high-consequence dangerous goods must adhere to a comprehensive security plan. This plan should include the following elements: 1. Assignment of Responsibilities: Clearly designate security responsibilities to competent and qualified individuals who possess the necessary authority to fulfill their duties effectively. 2. Record-Keeping: Maintain detailed records of the dangerous goods being transported, including their types and quantities. 3. Operational Review and Vulnerability Assessment: Conduct thorough reviews of current operations and assess vulnerabilities, particularly during intermodal transfers, temporary storage, handling, and distribution. 4. Security Measures and Training: Define specific security measures, including training policies for personnel. This should cover responses to elevated threat levels, verification of new employees, and restricted access to dangerous goods in proximity to vulnerable infrastructure. 5. Incident Reporting and Response Procedures: Establish effective and up-to-date procedures for reporting and addressing security threats, breaches, or incidents. 6. Evaluation and Testing of Security Plans: Implement procedures for the regular evaluation, testing, and updating of security plans to ensure their effectiveness. 7. Protection of Transport Information: Ensure the security of transport-related information contained within the plan and limit its distribution to the extent possible, while still complying with documentation requirements. Stakeholders in the Transport of Infectious Substances: Shipper (Consignor): Responsible for the correct identification, classification, packaging, marking, labeling, and documentation of infectious substances. They must ensure compliance with national and international regulations, confirm legal exportation, and coordinate with the receiver to ensure readiness for receipt. They must also prepare the shipment in accordance with packaging manufacturer instructions and arrange transport with the carrier, ensuring direct routing where possible. Packaging Supplier: Manufactures and tests packaging materials in compliance with regulations. They provide test reports and instructions to users to ensure proper use and performance. If required, they must be registered with a quality assurance program as directed by national authorities. Operator/Carrier: Includes logistics companies, couriers, and freight forwarders. They may advise the shipper on documentation and packaging, assist in arranging direct routing, and maintain records of shipment documentation. Receiver (Consignee): Confirms with national authorities the legal importation of the substance and obtains necessary permits. They arrange timely collection upon arrival and acknowledge receipt to the sender. Training Requirements for Dangerous Goods Transport: All personnel involved in the preparation and transport of dangerous goods must receive training to fulfill their responsibilities. This includes general awareness training, function-specific training, and safety training. Training content should align with the individual's assigned roles and responsibilities, as determined by their employer or national authorities. Training must be periodically supplemented with retraining, typically every two years, and records of training must be maintained and made available upon request. Classification of Infectious Substances: 1. Cultures: Concentrated collections of biological agents intentionally propagated under controlled conditions. If capable of causing disease in humans or animals, they are classified as infectious substances. 2. Patient Specimens: Materials collected directly from humans or animals for research or diagnostic purposes. If they contain disease-causing biological agents, they are classified as infectious substances. 3. Biological Products: Substances derived from living organisms (e.g., bacteria, fungi, vaccines) used for therapeutic, diagnostic, or preventive purposes. Some may be subject to additional regulations due to their importance in disease treatment and prevention. 4. Infected Live Animals: Animals infected with biological agents must be transported in compliance with regulations specific to their country of origin, transit, and destination. Live animals must not be used as a means of transporting infectious substances unless no other method is feasible. 5. Medical or Clinical Wastes: Contaminated waste generated during patient treatment or laboratory activities. If containing infectious agents, they are classified as infectious substances and assigned appropriate UN numbers (e.g., UN 2814, UN 2900, UN 3549). 6. Medical Devices or Equipment: Contaminated devices or equipment containing infectious agents capable of causing disease are classified as infectious substances. Special Considerations: Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) or microorganisms (GMMOs) that do not meet the definition of toxic or infectious substances are assigned to UN 3245. COVID-19 vaccines containing GMOs or GMMOs are not subject to Dangerous Goods Regulations.
